transcript:
## Personal Background and Family History

Douglas Leaman grew up in the Bible Presbyterian Church. He was born in Brazil while his family lived on the property where he now conducts his ministry. The family came to the United States when he was about seven or eight years old. After schooling, he attended The Master's College and Western Seminary before being commissioned to missionary work.

Pastor Leaman is married to Leah and has seven sons: Darius, Zayn, Titus, Solomon, Lucas, Roman, and Silas. Several of the younger boys were born in Brazil and have experienced the challenges of the climate there, particularly struggling with the cold when visiting the United States.

## Personal Testimony of Faith

When asked how he came to believe in Jesus Christ as his Savior, Pastor Leaman shared: "By God's grace, I have one of those super boring testimonies of growing up in a Christian home with a dad who is a pastor. I learned the gospel message and story from the very beginning. As a little kid, I remember praying in my bed and kind of recycling that prayer often as a young child. The spirit of God transformed my heart. I really don't know exactly how or when, but there was a constant realization of the importance of God and being his child from the beginning of my recollection."

This testimony was affirmed as a "glorious" testimony rather than a boring one—the testimony of a child raised in faith who experienced genuine transformation through God's Spirit.

## Overcoming the Fear of Man

In his teenage and college years, Pastor Leaman struggled significantly with the fear of man, social anxiety, and shyness. He explained: "In Brazil, this kind of thing was not well understood. There wasn't a good background of biblical thought on these issues. The first time I heard about it was that my shyness or what you would call social phobia or social anxiety could have a spiritual component was in college through Wayne Mack's teachings."

Mack had written extensively about the fear of man and its spiritual dimensions. As a young man, Leaman loved basketball, and he began to recognize that much of his passion for sports was connected to seeking glory, honor, and respect from men. He explains: "I loved basketball so much, and I began to understand through the years why I loved sports so much. I saw it was connected to seeking glory and honor and respect of men for my own life. Through sports, I was trying to get that."

This realization led him to write a thesis on playing sports to the glory of God. He now uses this personal struggle to counsel others: "Since I struggled with it so deeply, I feel I'm an expert with the fear of man. When counseling people with anxiety, I can connect it with theology, showing how the fear of man, anxiety, and pride are all interrelated."

He shared a powerful example of recent ministry: "I counseled a young man in his 30s with a wife and children who had a super intense struggle with anxiety. He's a deacon in a Reformed Presbyterian church. When he first heard about how the fear of the Lord addresses the fear of man, and how it connects to pride and anxiety, it just clicked for him. After decades of pharmaceutical treatment, he was transformed by God's grace in just a session or two. He still struggles, but now he understands the root issue."

## Calling to Ministry and Biblical Counseling

Growing up in a Christian home with reformed Presbyterian theology and teaching about God's sovereignty, Pastor Leaman developed a growing sense of the importance of serving the Lord. He attended seminary where he discovered the field of biblical counseling.

"This whole area of biblical counseling was presented to me, and I had never really thought about it before. It was almost a lost discipline, even within reformed churches. But then Jay Adams led a revival and reawakening to the church about biblical counseling. When I connected that field with my own internal struggles, I found it so valuable. Psychology is the number one studied subject in the world because man is interesting and everyone has struggles. To see that there are solutions in Christ and the gospel was profoundly interesting to me."

He continued: "I struggled internally and would have definitely been diagnosed with social anxiety disorder and put on medications. But to see the liberating power of the gospel and how God reaches into the depth of soul and heart was profoundly interesting. I found that my deep theological background in reformed Presbyterian theology had a hole in it—this whole area of biblical counseling was missing. I thought it very important and needy."

## God's Calling Through Injury

Pastor Leaman was an exceptional basketball player. He was part of the Brazilian national team for the 1996 Atlanta Olympics and played through the pre-tournament season. However, at age 25 or 26, he experienced a catastrophic knee injury during an intense game in Rio de Janeiro.

He reflects: "Everything I was resting my life on was suddenly gone. My fame, my finances, my acceptability—all gone. That's what I had put my life effort into. The Lord threw me out of basketball right at the critical time when I was about 25 or 26. If it had happened later, when I had more children and greater responsibilities, it would have been much harder. But it happened at just the right time so I could pursue seminary."

This injury taught him about idolatry: "I'm reminded every single day with pain in every movement of the folly of idol worship."

## Ministry Location and Context

Pastor Leaman and his family serve in northeast Brazil, in and around Aldeia, near the city of Recife. This is the farthest east you can go in South America—the closest point to Africa from the Americas. During World War II, the United States built a military base there to enable rapid crossing of the Atlantic.

He explains the context: "We live about 10 miles from downtown Recife, but the traffic is so intense—like I-5 rush hour getting to Seattle every single day. Just to travel 10 miles is a big task."

The location has unique characteristics: "In Brazil, everyone lives in the city. There are thousands of high rises in Recife alone, and in São Paulo you can literally fly for hours over high towers. This changes life completely—it changes demography and all sorts of things. By God's grace, we were able to escape that. We lived in an apartment for years, but now we have a house with a little bit of land."

## The Property and Its History

The property where Pastor Leaman's ministry is based has deep historical significance. His parents were called to care for an orphanage on this property run by the Presbyterian Church of Brazil. This is where Pastor Leaman was born.

When the missionary board PMU asked him to develop the property, he initially resisted: "The mission board was very clear that we were not going to focus on the orphanage land. Even though I was born there, the directors said, 'What do you think about using this property? We don't have any vision or focus for it currently, but we have six business guys who are directors. The land is owned in trust with a board of directors, not by an individual. Would you be interested in developing it?'"

After much negotiation, they secured a 15-year lease: "We argued with them and got it for 15 years. It was a pretty big battle to get everyone to see this could be something good. They saw my desire and passion—maybe my stubbornness—and came on board. Together with PMU and the Brazil Presbyterian Church, we stepped out in faith on this."

## The Soledale Gloria Institute of Technology and Theology

The centerpiece of Pastor Leaman's ministry is a unique gap year program called the Soledale Gloria Institute of Technology and Theology. This program brings together two areas that are typically separated: intensive theological training and practical technology education.

"We have an Institute of Technology and Theology called the Soledale Gloria Institute. In the States, it's kind of what you would call a gap year program, which doesn't really exist in Brazil. We're bringing something new there. We select twenty young men, ages 18 to 25, from pastors all over the country. Pastors recommend young men who are graduating from high school, don't know exactly what they want to do, but are committed to the church. We invite them for free—it's free to the students."

The program structure is intense: "They have one year of intense theological discipleship. We try to pack it all in in one year. But they also learn coding and technology. The idea is that technology can support ministry. We encourage them to go to the mission field—not as pastors necessarily, but as support staff. If you're coding, you can code from anywhere. You can work in country, provide critical mass for pastors planting churches, and earn income as well. They're not mandated to do that, but they're encouraged. And most of them have a job right after finishing their training."

The daily schedule combines multiple disciplines: "They study technology in the morning, theology in the afternoon. Every day they work on the land for an hour and a half. Manual labor is almost unknown for most Brazilian kids. Kids don't work at all in Brazil. But to take care of animals and plant seeds—that's an old American work ethic I learned from my dad growing up. Brazil stuff grows. It rains and there's sunshine all year round. So it's a great place to implement that. After that hour and a half of work, they do an hour of weightlifting or sports."

The program has been remarkably successful: "We've had ninety guys go through the program now. They're getting married, having kids. It's kind of fun to see that gathering and hopefully a gathering of good godly men who can help bring growth and strengthening to the nation."

## Additional Ministry Activities

Beyond the institute, the property hosts multiple ministry functions:

**Church Rentals:** "Churches use the property for their weekend events, whether for evangelism or strengthening through a day of fellowship. A lot of churches rent the property. We've finally gotten to a place where we're moving in the direction of being self-sustaining. For that to happen, we really need to have it rented every weekend from Friday to Saturday. Ideally we'll get there, but it's running at about 50% of the year now, and every year it's growing."

**Pastor Training:** "We bring pastors back, especially pastors from the interior or countryside areas where they have a really difficult time going to the city by themselves. We have a big place so we can house them, train them for a week, give them a lot of information and modules, and let them take it back to the interior."

**Camps:** "We provide our own camps as well. I think we did six or seven this year, which was by far the most intense. We do English camps. Some of you have been there. Some of the youth have come to Brazil for English camp. That's all amazing."

**Café Ministry:** "My wife Leah runs a café at the property to help fund the project. She sells American stuff like apple pies and cinnamon rolls—stuff you really can't get in that culture. It's super special and people are coming from the city, facing rough roads to get there. She's helping the project a lot."

## Challenges and Blessings

Pastor Leaman acknowledged the difficulties of the location: "The roads are a real challenge. The roads are not paved, and when it rains for months, they just become full of mud. A new car can only last about five years. The last two miles to where we live are particularly rough. You need a chiropractor adjustment just from driving down the hill."

Regarding his calling to stay in this difficult context: "As long as I really feel and believe that the Lord is using the ministry in a way to make impact, I'm committed. If you face so many difficulties in so many different areas of life—and socialism is a heavy burden—you can't sustain it unless you feel like you're being used. If you don't feel like you're being used despite all the hardships, you have to get out quick, because you just melt inside. But when you're feeling used and have opportunity to do discipleship and training, it sustains you."

## Financial Support and Future Plans

Pastor Leaman expressed deep gratitude for the financial support from his supporting congregation: "You guys are definitely sending and our main support is financial. This is a huge encouragement. When the project doesn't have funds, I can't just say we won't pay the workers this month. We have a lot of workers now and I'm responsible for that. So you guys helping with the project helps me face that intense pressure. We're so thankful for that. The way you guys have stepped in to participate, with youth coming to English camp—that's all amazing. The prayers are the main ways, and I couldn't ask for more."

He explained the financial situation: "Our church supports about $36,000 a year between supporting my family's income and the project itself. Money is always the answer to this question, but there are other ways to help as well. Prayers are crucial. We also have another responsibility—we're helping support Pastor Dennis and Lucy, who have received my boys into their home. That's another $30,000 a year."

Regarding future plans: "I'm 53 years old. I think I have another 12-15 years in me, as long as Leah can hang in there with me. We've recently taken on more responsibility with an additional property in God Avatar, about two and a half to three hour drive up in the mountains. It's a beautiful property, but right now it's just an expense for us. We're trying to get that transferred and sold. That would be an amazing prayer because it would help us finish some projects on our land and build some buildings."

## Vision for Christ and the Gospel

When asked what he has learned about Christ through serving in Brazil, Pastor Leaman offered this vision:

"The sovereignty of God and the importance of Christ and His word, the gospel, the church for all of life—these are paramount. Knowing Christ is important not just for individuals, but for marriages, families, local churches, and then even beyond. It's been one of my passions to see Christ applied to all these levels.

"You guys live in the most blessed, rich, wealthy place in the history of the world. When you step out of that and see the burdensome economic situations in other places, you want to ask: How can you help? I see the solutions in Christ and the wisdom of Christ. There's an all-encompassing need for the proclamation of Christ and His word for individuals, cultures, and countries as well. Thanks for the privilege of allowing me to do that and partnering with me when you send missionaries. You allow us to work and try to help bring the word of Christ to lands that don't have the wealth and riches that we enjoy. And may we not lose that hope."
